pairs: Fine art portraiture — the direct reference to painting tradition
Dramatic single-source lighting — one light, deep shadows
Dark backgrounds — the subject floats in darkness
Warm key light + cool shadows — amplifies the contrast
Still life — the classical genre for chiaroscuro
conflicts: Even/flat illumination — chiaroscuro requires extremes
Modern/minimal aesthetics — the style is baroque and dramatic
High-key brightness — the opposite approach
terms.example: Chiaroscuro + single warm key light from above-left + dark background + still life with fruit and metal → objects glowing against deep darkness, rich warm highlights, cool shadow tones, painterly dimensionality

extras.Landmark uses: Caravaggio's paintings (The Calling of St. Matthew — shaft of light as divine finger). Gregg Toland's cinematography in **Citizen Kane** (1941). Gordon Willis in **The Godfather**. Stanley Kubrick's **Barry Lyndon** candlelight scenes. Roger Deakins in nearly every film — the master of motivated chiaroscuro.

terms.name: Silhouette
terms.what: Subject is completely backlit with no fill, rendering as a dark shape against a bright background. Only the outline is visible.
terms.effect: Graphic, bold, anonymous. The subject loses all detail and becomes pure shape. The viewer's attention goes to form, posture, and outline. Emotional content comes from body language and context rather than facial expression.
pairs: Sunset/sunrise backgrounds — the classic silhouette scenario
Strong, recognizable shapes — the outline must read clearly
Dramatic/emotional moments — the anonymity amplifies universal feeling
Wide angle — silhouette against expansive sky
Bold color in the background — the dark shape against vivid color is graphic
conflicts: Facial detail or expression — completely lost
Product visibility — the subject is black
Subtle lighting nuance — silhouette is binary: lit or not
terms.example: Silhouette + sunset + figure standing on cliff edge + wide angle → black shape against orange/purple gradient sky, dramatic outline, epic scale, anonymous but emotional

terms.name: Overexposed / Blown Highlights
terms.what: Intentionally pushing exposure so highlights clip to pure white. Detail is lost in the brightest areas — skin glows, windows blow out, light sources wash out.
terms.effect: Dreamy, ethereal, luminous. The blown areas create a glow that bleeds into surrounding tones. Reads as romantic, nostalgic, or deliberately imperfect. Common in film photography where highlight rolloff is gradual.
pairs: Film aesthetics — overexposure is a film characteristic
Backlit subjects — the background blows out, subject glows at edges
Soft/romantic mood — the brightness and glow feel tender
Polaroid/instant aesthetic — overexposure is part of the look
High-key with intention — bright but with character, not clinical
conflicts: Detail recovery — the information is gone in blown areas
Dark/moody work — the brightness fights it
Precise, controlled rendering — overexposure is inherently loose

terms.name: Crushed Blacks / Underexposed
terms.what: Shadow areas pushed to pure black with no detail. The opposite of blown highlights. Deliberate loss of shadow information.
terms.effect: Heavy, weighty, dramatic. Dark areas become pure black voids. The remaining lit areas feel more intense by contrast. Reads as moody, serious, or film noir-influenced.
pairs: Film noir / low-key — crushed blacks are the signature
High contrast black and white — extremes of the tonal range
Dramatic single-source lighting — shadows go completely dark
Desaturated or monochromatic palettes — the darkness dominates
conflicts: Shadow detail — it's gone
Bright/airy moods — too heavy
Even/balanced exposure — crushed blacks are a deliberate imbalance
terms.example: Crushed blacks + single hard key from side + tight crop on face + black and white → half the face illuminated, other half pure black void, extreme contrast, graphic weight

terms.name: Candlelight (~1,850K)
terms.effect: Very warm, orange, flickering. Intimate, romantic, low-light. Faces glow warmly. Shadows are deep and warm.
pairs: Intimate scenes, period/historical settings, romantic mood, warm skin tones.

terms.name: Tungsten / Incandescent (~2,400-3,200K)
terms.effect: Warm, amber, steady. The classic indoor light before LEDs. Cozy, domestic, nostalgic. Everything has an amber cast.
pairs: Interior scenes, cozy/homey mood, nostalgic/vintage, warm portraits.

terms.name: Daylight (~5,500K)
terms.effect: Neutral, balanced. No strong warm or cool bias. The "standard" that everything else is compared against. Clean and natural.
pairs: Product photography (accurate color), documentary, outdoor scenes at midday.

terms.name: Overcast / Shade (~6,500-7,500K)
terms.effect: Slightly cool, blue-ish. Somber, muted, contemplative. The cool cast can make images feel melancholy or clinical.
pairs: Melancholy mood, muted palettes, overcast landscapes, cool skin tones.

terms.name: Blue Hour / Deep Shade (~8,000-10,000K+)
terms.effect: Strongly cool, blue. The color of twilight and deep shadow. Ethereal, cold, quiet.
pairs: Cityscapes at twilight, cold/winter scenes, moody portraits, noir.

terms.name: Loop Lighting
terms.what: Key light placed ~30-45 degrees to the side and slightly above the subject. Named for the small loop-shaped shadow it casts from the nose onto the cheek. The shadow does NOT connect to the cheek shadow (that would be Rembrandt).
terms.effect: Gentle dimensionality. More sculpted than flat/butterfly but softer than Rembrandt. Universally flattering — the most commonly used portrait lighting pattern because it works on virtually any face shape.
pairs: Soft light modifiers — softbox, beauty dish
Fill light at 2:1 ratio — controlled but not dramatic
Window light — natural loop from a side window
Headshots/corporate portraiture — the standard safe choice
conflicts: Hard light without fill — pushes toward Rembrandt
Extremely low angles — destroys the loop pattern
Maximum drama — too gentle

terms.name: Broad Lighting
terms.what: Key light illuminates the side of the face turned TOWARD the camera. The broader (more visible) plane of the face is lit.
terms.effect: Face appears wider. More of the face is in light than shadow. Open, approachable feel. Used to add visual weight to narrow faces.
pairs: High key — bright, even, approachable
Soft light — gentle and flattering
Subjects with narrow/thin faces — adds visual width
Commercial/corporate work — open and welcoming
conflicts: Subjects with wide/round faces — makes them look wider
Low key drama — undermines the shadow depth
Short lighting — the exact opposite approach

terms.name: Short Lighting
terms.what: Key light illuminates the side of the face turned AWAY from camera. The narrower (less visible) plane of the face is lit. The shadow side faces the camera.
terms.effect: Face appears thinner and more sculpted. More shadow on the camera-facing side creates depth and drama. Slimming effect. More moody than broad.
pairs: Low key — dramatic, shadow-dominant
Rembrandt lighting — short + Rembrandt is the classic dramatic portrait
Subjects with round faces — slimming effect
Moody/artistic portraiture
conflicts: High key — the shadow dominance fights even brightness
Flat commercial looks — too sculpted
Broad lighting — the exact opposite

terms.name: Clamshell Lighting
terms.what: Two lights (or light + reflector) above and below the subject, creating a "clamshell." Key light above angled down, fill below angled up. Camera shoots through the gap.
terms.effect: Extremely even, flattering illumination. Minimizes wrinkles and texture. Catchlights appear at 12 and 6 o'clock in the eyes. Glamorous, polished, virtually shadowless on the face.
pairs: Beauty photography — the standard beauty setup
Makeup campaigns — even light shows color accurately
Beauty dish (top) + silver reflector (bottom) — the classic combo
High key — clean, bright, flawless
Close-up portraits — the even light is most apparent close up
conflicts: Dramatic/moody looks — too even and flattering
Masculine/gritty portraits — too polished
Environmental portraits — needs controlled distance
terms.example: Clamshell lighting + beauty dish overhead + silver reflector below chin + macro beauty close-up → virtually shadowless, dewy skin, dual catchlights, glamorous and flawless

terms.name: Hair Light / Kicker
terms.what: Light placed behind and above (hair light) or behind and to the side (kicker) of the subject. Part of the extended three-point family. Specifically targets hair, shoulders, or edge of the subject for separation.
terms.effect: Luminous rim on hair and shoulders. Adds a third dimension by separating subject from background. Hair light is overhead/behind; kicker is from the side, adding a slash of light on cheek/jaw.
pairs: Three-point lighting — the third point
Dark backgrounds — essential for separation when background is dark
Portrait photography — defines the subject's outline
Rim light — closely related, hair light is a specific application
conflicts: High key with white backgrounds — separation already exists
Naturalistic/available light — the precision looks artificial
Flat/front-lit setups — the back light has no role

terms.name: Practical Lighting
terms.what: Using visible, in-scene light sources as actual contributing lights — table lamps, candles, neon signs, TV screens, car headlights, streetlights. Not just props but real sources that shape the image.
terms.effect: Deeply naturalistic and cinematic. The audience sees where the light comes from. Creates pools of warm, localized light with natural falloff. Strong sense of place and atmosphere.
pairs: Motivated lighting — practicals provide the "motivation"
Warm color temperature — most practical sources are warm
Shallow depth of field — practical light sources become bokeh when out of focus
Film noir — desk lamps, streetlights as scene illumination
Intimate scenes — the localized light creates intimacy
CineStill 800T — the halation effect on practicals is the iconic shot
conflicts: High key — practicals create pools, not floods
Clean commercial looks — the light is uneven and warm
Even illumination — practicals fall off quickly
terms.example: Practical lighting + tungsten desk lamp in frame + warm glow + shallow depth of field + dark moody interior → naturalistic, cinematic, warm pool of light, face lit by the lamp in the scene

extras.Landmark use: **Barry Lyndon** (1975) — Kubrick's candlelight scenes lit by actual candles only (NASA f/0.7 lens, 3 candela average illumination). The definitive example of practical lighting in cinema.

terms.name: Motivated Lighting
terms.what: Studio or off-camera lighting placed and shaped to appear as though it comes from a visible or implied source in the scene. The light is "motivated" by a window, lamp, or the sun — even if the actual illumination is supplemented or replaced by studio lights.
terms.effect: Naturalistic but controlled. Looks like available light but with cinematic precision. The audience never questions where the light comes from. Roger Deakins and Emmanuel Lubezki are masters of this approach.
pairs: Practical lighting — practicals provide the visible "motivation"
Window light simulation — large soft source from one side
Golden hour simulation — warm directional light from low angle
Naturalistic drama — the Deakins approach
Interior scenes — every light has a "reason"
conflicts: Obviously artificial setups — ring light, colored gels without a source
Unmotivated colored light — color from nowhere breaks the illusion
High-key product lighting — no visible source to motivate from

terms.name: Available / Ambient Light (Deliberate Choice)
terms.what: Choosing to use ONLY the existing light in a scene — no added lighting. Includes both natural light and existing artificial sources (fluorescents, streetlights). A deliberate artistic and technical choice.
terms.effect: Maximum authenticity. Often uneven, mixed color temperatures, unpredictable. Documentary feel. Can be stunning or challenging depending on conditions.
pairs: Fast lenses (f/1.2-f/2) — wide aperture gathers the available light
High ISO / visible grain — the tradeoff for shooting in low light
Documentary / street photography — the authentic look
Photojournalism — capturing what's there, not what you set up
conflicts: Controlled studio looks — the opposite approach
Precise exposure requirements — available light is unpredictable
Beauty/commercial demanding consistency — too variable

terms.name: Beauty Dish
terms.what: Parabolic metal dish with a deflector plate blocking direct light, bouncing it off the dish interior before reaching the subject. Between hard and soft — more contrast than softbox, more wrap than bare bulb.
terms.effect: "Poppy" light with moderate contrast. Defined but not harsh shadows. Specular highlights that bring out skin texture and contour. Distinctive round catchlight. The signature modifier for fashion and beauty photography.
pairs: Clamshell setups — beauty dish on top, reflector below
Butterfly lighting pattern — the classic beauty dish position
Fashion editorial — the contrasty quality reads as editorial
Athletic/fitness portraits — the moderate contrast sculpts muscle
Close-up beauty — the quality is most apparent close
conflicts: Ultra-soft glamour — too much contrast
Documentary/naturalistic — too precise and artificial
Large groups — the falloff is significant

terms.name: Softbox
terms.what: Enclosed modifier with internal baffles and a front diffusion panel. Creates a large, even, wrapped light source. The larger the softbox relative to the subject, the softer the light.
terms.effect: Soft, gradual shadow transitions. Wraparound illumination that gently sculpts. Rectangular or octagonal catchlights. Flattering and forgiving of skin texture. The workhorse modifier.
pairs: Portrait photography — universally flattering
Product photography — even, clean illumination
Loop and butterfly patterns — the soft quality suits gentle shadow shapes
High key — large softboxes fill the scene with soft light
conflicts: Hard-light drama — softboxes eliminate it
Film noir — need crisp, defined shadows
Gobo/cookie work — destroys the pattern edges

terms.name: Fresnel
terms.what: Light with a Fresnel lens (concentric ridged glass) that produces a controllable beam from tight spot to wide flood. The signature look of classic Hollywood and theater lighting.
terms.effect: Semi-hard light with slightly softened edges — not razor-sharp like a bare bulb, not diffused like a softbox. Clean, defined shadows with a cinematic quality. Controllable beam spread.
pairs: Motivated lighting — the controlled beam can be aimed precisely
Film/cinema setups — the classic cinematic light
Rembrandt and loop patterns — the semi-hard quality is ideal
Three-point lighting — designed for this setup
Dramatic/theatrical looks
conflicts: Ultra-soft beauty looks — needs additional diffusion
Ring light aesthetics — completely different quality
Broad, even wash — Fresnels are directional

terms.name: Gobo / Cookie Lighting (Patterned Shadows)
terms.what: A "gobo" (go-between) or "cucoloris" (cookie) placed between a light source and the subject to create patterned shadows. Window blinds, tree branches, lace, custom cut patterns.
terms.effect: Dappled, textured light. Suggests an environment without showing it — blinds imply a noir office, branches imply a forest, lace implies romance. Breaks up flat surfaces and adds visual complexity.
pairs: Hard light — sharp, defined patterns
Film noir — venetian blind shadows are the genre's signature
Golden hour — branch shadows from the low sun
Motivated lighting — the pattern implies a source
Chiaroscuro — patterned light on a dark scene
conflicts: Soft/diffused light — blurs and destroys the pattern edges
Clean commercial looks — the shadows are distracting
Beauty close-ups — patterns across the face can be unflattering (unless intentional editorial)
terms.example: Gobo through venetian blinds + hard key + low key + subject at desk → noir shadow stripes across face and wall, implied window source, dramatic tension

terms.name: Negative Fill
terms.what: Using a black flag, V-flat, or dark surface to SUBTRACT light from one side of the subject. The opposite of fill light — deepens shadows by preventing ambient bounce.
terms.effect: Increased contrast on one side without adding a second light. Darker, more sculpted shadows. Creates drama with a single source by controlling where light does NOT go.
pairs: Window light portraits — black V-flat opposite the window
Single key setups — negative fill adds contrast without more lights
Editorial/moody portraits — controlled shadow depth
Soft key light — negative fill adds drama to an otherwise gentle source
conflicts: High key — negative fill removes light, high key adds it
Flat/even illumination — the goal is the opposite
Bright/airy aesthetics — too dark on one side

terms.name: Barn Doors / Flags / Snoots
terms.what: Subtractive tools that narrow, shape, or block a light beam. Barn doors attach to the light; flags are freestanding; snoots concentrate light into a narrow beam. Control where light falls and where it doesn't.
terms.effect: Precise light placement. Pools of light on specific areas. Light on the face but not the background (or vice versa). Theatrical precision.
pairs: Dramatic portraits — isolated pools of light
Film noir — precise, theatrical control
Spotlight effects — snoots create narrow beams
Any setup requiring spill control
conflicts: Broad, even wash — these tools restrict light
Natural/ambient approaches — too controlled

terms.name: Top Light / Overhead
terms.what: Light directly above the subject pointing straight down. Creates deep shadows in eye sockets, under nose and chin. Used for oppressive, spiritual, or ominous moods.
terms.effect: "Raccoon eyes" — deep eye socket shadows. Lit crown and shoulders, dark face. Ominous or spiritual depending on context. Think the Godfather baptism scene or cathedral light from above.
pairs: Low key — dark, dramatic, oppressive
Religious/spiritual scenes — light from heaven
Horror — the shadow-filled eyes are unsettling
Dramatic film — power and authority
conflicts: Flattering portraiture — deeply unflattering on most faces
Commercial/beauty — the eye shadows are too deep
Even illumination — the opposite approach

terms.name: Under Lighting / Uplighting
terms.what: Light from below the subject pointing up. The "flashlight under the chin" effect. Reverses all normal shadow patterns.
terms.effect: Unnatural, horror-coded. Every shadow is wrong — under the brow instead of above, above the chin instead of below. The reversal triggers subconscious unease because we never see faces lit from below in nature. Used for villain reveals, campfire scenes, supernatural moments.
pairs: Horror/thriller — the unsettling shadow reversal
Campfire/bonfire scenes — the natural justification for uplighting
Villain/monster reveals — classic horror movie technique
Warm practical sources at table level — candles, campfires
Green/cool color gels — amplifies the unnatural quality
conflicts: Naturalistic portraiture — the shadows are wrong
Beauty/flattering light — deeply unflattering
Daytime/outdoor — no natural source from below

terms.name: Book Lighting
terms.what: A two-step diffusion technique: light hits a bounce surface, then the bounced light passes through a diffusion frame. Named because the bounce + diffusion panels resemble an open book. A favorite of cinematographer Robert Richardson.
terms.effect: Extremely soft, luminous, virtually shadowless quality. The ultimate in gentle, wrapping light. Retains a subtle directionality that pure diffusion can lose. Used for intimate close-ups where skin must look flawless.
pairs: Close-up beauty — the softest possible light
Intimate dialogue scenes — gentle, wrapping
Motivated window light — the setup can simulate a large window
Cinematic portraits — the quality is distinctly filmic
conflicts: Hard-light looks — the opposite approach
Film noir — no shadow structure
High-energy/edgy aesthetics — too gentle

terms.name: Cross Lighting
terms.what: Two light sources on opposite sides of the subject, each lighting one half. Neither is clearly dominant — they can be equal or slightly varied in intensity.
terms.effect: Strong dimensionality from both sides. Central shadow line down the middle of the face/subject. Dramatic and sculptural. Creates tension or conflict in narrative work — the dual sources imply opposing forces.
pairs: Dramatic scenes — the dual opposition creates tension
Sports photography — dynamic, dimensional
Hard light sources — defined central shadow
Theatrical/stage lighting — the dramatic split
conflicts: Beauty/flat lighting — too sculptural
Single-source naturalism — two visible sources fight naturalism
Soft glamour — too dramatic

terms.name: Tent / Wraparound Lighting
terms.what: Subject enclosed or nearly enclosed in diffusion material, with lights firing through from outside. Common in product photography. Virtually shadowless, even illumination from all directions.
terms.effect: No visible shadows. Perfectly even illumination. Reflective surfaces show clean gradual gradients instead of hot spots. Clinical and pristine.
pairs: Product photography — jewelry, bottles, reflective objects
Catalog/e-commerce work — clean, even, consistent
High key white background — the standard product setup
Reflective objects — eliminates hot spots
conflicts: Any portrait work wanting dimension — completely flat
Mood lighting — no shadow, no mood
Dramatic composition — everything is even

terms.name: Kodak Portra 160
terms.what: Professional color negative, ISO 160. The finest-grain Portra. Daylight balanced. Introduced 1998, updated 2010.
terms.effect: Extremely fine grain, almost invisible in normal prints. Balanced, natural color saturation — not punchy, not muted. Skin tones are the priority: warm, accurate, dimensional. Highlight rolloff is gentle — overexposed areas fade gracefully rather than clipping hard. The overall look is polished, clean, and natural.
pairs: Studio/controlled light — the low ISO needs plenty of light
Medium format — fine grain + large negative = almost grainless, creamy images
Beauty and fashion — skin tone accuracy is the core strength
Soft directional light — the gentle tonality shines in subtle gradations
85mm portrait lens — the classic Portra portrait setup
conflicts: Low light / available light — ISO 160 needs bright conditions or flash
Gritty/raw aesthetic — too clean and polished
High contrast drama — Portra is gentle, not dramatic
terms.example: Portra 160 + Hasselblad + soft window light + 80mm f/2.8 → creamy, virtually grainless portrait, warm natural skin tones, gentle highlight rolloff, medium format richness

terms.name: Kodak Portra 400
terms.what: Professional color negative, ISO 400. The most popular Portra — versatile enough for studio and available light. The default "film look" in modern photography.
terms.effect: Very fine grain, visible at large prints but never intrusive. Same skin tone priority as 160 but with slightly more grain texture. Warm midtones, muted but not desaturated color palette. The highlight rolloff is famously beautiful — overexposed Portra 400 has a warm, golden, dreamy quality that's become the defining "film aesthetic" on social media. Slight pastel quality in the shadows.
pairs: Overexposure (+1 to +2 stops) — the highlight rolloff is the signature move, overexposed Portra is a genre
Golden hour — the warm cast amplifies Portra's warmth
Wedding/lifestyle photography — the romantic, warm quality defines the genre
35mm — the grain adds character without being heavy
Available light — ISO 400 handles most daylight conditions
conflicts: Cool/clinical color palettes — Portra is inherently warm
Punchy/saturated color — Portra is muted by design
High-contrast graphic work — the gentle tonal curve softens everything
terms.example: Portra 400 + overexposed +1 stop + golden hour backlight + 35mm → warm, dreamy, grain visible but gentle, blown highlights with golden glow, the definitive "film look"

terms.name: Kodak Portra 800
terms.what: Professional color negative, ISO 800. The fast Portra — designed for low light while maintaining the Portra color science.
terms.effect: More visible grain than 160/400 but still controlled. Same warm skin tone priority. Slightly more contrast than slower Portras. The grain adds texture and grit while maintaining the characteristic warmth. Works in conditions where 160 and 400 can't.
pairs: Low light / indoor available light — the core use case
Evening/dusk shooting — enough speed for fading light
Concert/event photography — fast enough for handheld in dim venues
Grain as texture — the visible grain is a feature at this speed
conflicts: Studio/controlled light — overkill, use 160 or 400 for cleaner results
Ultra-clean rendering — grain is visible and present
Large format — Portra 800 is mainly a 35mm and 120 stock

terms.name: Kodak Ektar 100
terms.what: Consumer/prosumer color negative, ISO 100. The world's finest-grain color negative film. Daylight balanced.
terms.effect: Ultra-fine grain, extremely high saturation and color punch. Much more vivid than Portra — reds are fiery, blues are deep, greens are electric. High contrast with strong tonal separation. Skin tones lean slightly red/warm and can look oversaturated compared to Portra. This is a landscape and product film, not a portrait film.
pairs: Landscape — saturated color is the point, and the fine grain holds detail
Product/still life — vivid, punchy color representation
Bright daylight — ISO 100 needs full sun
Graphic/bold compositions — the high saturation supports bold visual statements
conflicts: Flattering skin tones — Ektar oversaturates skin, especially reds
Muted/pastel color — Ektar is the opposite of muted
Low light — ISO 100, needs bright conditions
terms.example: Ektar 100 + midday sun + landscape + wide angle + f/11 → punchy saturated greens and blues, deep shadows, vivid sky, ultra-fine grain, maximum color impact

terms.name: Kodak Gold 200
terms.what: Consumer color negative, ISO 200. The ubiquitous "yellow box" film. Cheap, accessible, the film most people grew up with.
terms.effect: Warm, slightly amber/golden cast. Moderate grain — visible but not heavy. Colors lean warm and slightly muted compared to professional stocks. A nostalgic, familiar quality — this is what family photos, vacation snapshots, and disposable camera pictures look like. The warmth is less refined than Portra: more golden/amber than creamy.
pairs: Nostalgia/memory — the film of childhood photos
Warm daylight — amplifies the golden cast
Snapshot/candid aesthetic — the consumer quality is the point
Point-and-shoot cameras — the intended pairing
conflicts: Professional precision — Gold is a consumer stock with looser tolerances
Cool/clinical tones — too warm and golden
Fine detail — the grain is present and consumer-grade

terms.name: Fuji Superia 400
terms.what: Consumer color negative, ISO 400. Fuji's answer to Kodak Gold but with different color science — cooler, greener.
terms.effect: Cooler tones than Kodak stocks — slight green/cyan cast in shadows, less warm overall. Moderate grain. Greens are vivid, skin tones lean slightly cool/neutral. The Fuji color palette is distinct from Kodak: where Kodak is warm and amber, Fuji is cool and green.
pairs: Green environments — foliage looks lush on Fuji stocks
Cooler/neutral mood — less warmth than Kodak
Urban/street — the cool cast suits concrete and mixed light
Overcast conditions — the cool film + cool light creates a unified tone
conflicts: Warm/golden mood — Fuji is cooler by nature
Warm skin tones — the green cast can make skin look pallid
Sunset/golden hour warmth — fights the film's cool lean

terms.name: Kodachrome
terms.what: Kodak's legendary slide film. K-14 processing (unique, complex). Discontinued 2009, last roll processed December 30, 2010. Available in 25 and 64 ISO versions.
terms.effect: Rich, saturated but not garish color. Photographer Steve McCurry described it: "a great color palette... not too garish... more poetry in it, a softness, an elegance." Warm reds and yellows, deep but not electric blues. The colors feel real but heightened — a curated version of reality. Fine grain. The defining look of National Geographic magazine and mid-20th century color photography.
pairs: Documentary/travel — the National Geographic aesthetic
Warm daylight — Kodachrome's reds and yellows glow in sun
35mm — the classic Kodachrome format
Nostalgic mid-century color — this IS that look
Medium contrast scenes — Kodachrome handles them beautifully
conflicts: Available shooting — the film hasn't been manufactured since 2009
High contrast scenes — slide film's narrow latitude clips easily
Cool/desaturated palettes — Kodachrome is warm and vivid
terms.example: Kodachrome 64 + 35mm + travel/street scene + warm daylight → rich warm color with poetic saturation, fine grain, National Geographic quality, mid-century documentary warmth

terms.name: Fuji Velvia 50
terms.what: Professional slide film, ISO 50. The landscape photographer's film. E-6 processing. Still manufactured.
terms.effect: Extremely high color saturation — the most vivid of any slide film. Greens are electric, blues are deep and intense, reds are fiery. Very high contrast with strong tonal separation. Extremely fine grain with the highest resolving power of any slide film (160 lines/mm). The colors are heightened beyond natural but in a way that feels "more real than real." Where Kodachrome has poetry, Velvia has intensity.
pairs: Landscape — the defining landscape film
Bold saturated scenes — blue sky, green foliage, autumn colors
Golden hour and blue hour — the saturation amplifies the color drama
Large format — Velvia + 4x5 = maximum detail and color intensity
Deep depth of field — landscape compositions front to back
conflicts: Skin tones — Velvia oversaturates skin to an unnatural degree
Subtle/muted palettes — Velvia makes everything vivid
Low light — ISO 50 needs full sun or a tripod
Long exposures — Velvia suffers from reciprocity failure (color shift on long exposures)
terms.example: Velvia 50 + 4x5 large format + landscape + golden hour → explosively saturated sky and foliage, no visible grain, extreme sharpness front to back, the definitive landscape film look

terms.name: Fuji Provia 100F
terms.what: Professional slide film, ISO 100. E-6 processing. Fuji's "neutral" slide film — less saturated than Velvia, more versatile.
terms.effect: Accurate, natural color with moderate saturation — vivid but not hyper-real like Velvia. Extremely fine grain. Neutral color balance — neither warm (Kodachrome) nor ultra-vivid (Velvia). The "honest" slide film that renders things as they are. Good for subjects where accuracy matters more than impact.
pairs: Product/commercial — accurate color representation
Architecture — neutral rendering, fine detail
Any subject where color accuracy matters — Provia doesn't editorialize
Studio/controlled conditions — the neutral balance responds well to precise lighting
conflicts: Maximum impact/saturation — Velvia does that job
Warm nostalgic mood — Provia is neutral, not warm
Gritty/textured aesthetic — too clean and precise

terms.name: Kodak Tri-X 400
terms.what: The most iconic black and white film. ISO 400. Gelatin-silver process. Introduced ~1940. The film of photojournalism, street photography, and documentary. Still manufactured.
terms.effect: Pronounced, characterful grain — not fine, not coarse, distinctly "Tri-X." Rich mid-tones with strong blacks. High but not extreme contrast. Push-processable to 800, 1600, even 3200 with increasing grain and contrast. The grain has a chunky, organic quality that's immediately recognizable. This is what "black and white photography" looks like in the collective imagination.
pairs: Street photography — the combination of Tri-X + 35mm + 28-50mm lens IS street photography
Push processing — shooting at 800 or 1600 in low light, developing at a higher time, increases grain and contrast for a raw, urgent look
High contrast scenes — Tri-X handles the tonal extremes
Photojournalism/documentary — the film's heritage IS this genre
Hard/directional light — the contrast translates beautifully to B&W
conflicts: Fine grain/smooth tonal rendering — Tri-X is characterful, not smooth
Color (obviously) — but worth noting the "Tri-X look" implies monochrome
Delicate/ethereal mood — Tri-X is gritty and present
terms.example: Tri-X 400 pushed to 800 + 28mm + street scene + hard light → chunky grain, deep blacks, bright highlights, photojournalistic urgency, classic documentary energy

terms.name: Ilford HP5 Plus 400
terms.what: ISO 400 black and white film. Tri-X's main competitor. Gelatin-silver process. Push-processable to 3200. Introduced 1989.
terms.effect: Slightly smoother grain than Tri-X. Lower base contrast — more gradual tonal transitions. The shadows are more open (more detail in dark areas). Where Tri-X is punchy and contrasty, HP5 is smoother and more forgiving. Both have strong grain, but HP5's feels more even and less chunky.
pairs: Portraiture in B&W — the smoother tonality flatters more than Tri-X
Soft/overcast light — HP5's lower contrast suits gentle conditions
Push processing — handles it well with less contrast spike than Tri-X
General-purpose B&W — more versatile than the more opinionated Tri-X
conflicts: Maximum contrast/punch — Tri-X does that better
Ultra-fine grain — HP5 is still grainy at ISO 400
The "classic photojournalism" look — that's Tri-X territory culturally

terms.name: Ilford Delta 3200
terms.what: Ultra-high-speed black and white film. True ISO ~1000-1250, designed to be push-processed to 3200 or 6400. Tabular grain.
terms.effect: Heavy, prominent grain with a distinctive character. High contrast. The grain becomes a dominant visual element — the image is as much about texture as content. Deep blacks, chalky highlights. The look is raw, nocturnal, and urgent. This is the film for shooting in near-darkness.
pairs: Extreme low light — concerts, clubs, nighttime street
Grain as primary aesthetic — the texture IS the image
High contrast B&W — deep blacks against bright highlights
Raw/punk energy — the heavy grain reads as unpolished and urgent
35mm — the grain is already heavy; smaller format amplifies it
conflicts: Fine detail — the grain obscures it
Clean rendering — the opposite of this film's character
Controlled/studio work — overkill, use a slower film
terms.example: Delta 3200 + nighttime street + available light + 35mm → heavy grain, faces emerging from darkness, high contrast, raw nocturnal energy

terms.name: Ilford FP4 Plus 125
terms.what: ISO 125 fine-grain black and white film. The "careful" B&W film — where HP5 and Tri-X are fast and gritty, FP4 is slow and precise.
terms.effect: Very fine grain for a B&W film. Smooth tonal gradations — long scale from deep black to bright white with many shades between. Low contrast curve. The image is detailed, resolved, and deliberate. Reads as contemplative and precise.
pairs: Landscape in B&W — the fine grain holds detail, the tonal range captures gradations
Medium and large format — fine grain + big negative = virtually grainless
Studio/controlled light — the low ISO needs plenty of light
Architectural photography — detail and precision
Long exposure — FP4 handles reciprocity well
conflicts: Low light — ISO 125 needs bright conditions
Gritty/raw aesthetic — too refined
Action/movement — slow film + needed exposure = motion blur risk

terms.name: CineStill 800T
terms.what: Kodak Vision3 500T cinema film with the remjet anti-halation layer removed, repackaged for C-41 still photography processing. Tungsten balanced (3200K). ISO 800. Introduced 2012.
terms.effect: The signature look is **halation** — a red/orange glow around bright highlights (neon signs, street lights, candles) caused by the removed anti-halation layer. Light that would normally be absorbed scatters back through the red-sensitive layer, creating ethereal halos. Tungsten balance means daylight shots go blue unless corrected. Under tungsten/artificial light, colors are neutral and cinematic. High speed for low-light shooting. The overall look is nocturnal, cinematic, and dreamy.
pairs: Nighttime urban scenes — neon signs with halation halos are the iconic CineStill shot
Artificial/tungsten light — the film is balanced for it, colors render naturally
Cinematic mood — it IS cinema film, the motion picture color science carries over
Available light — ISO 800 handles dim conditions
Wet streets — reflections of halated lights multiply the effect
conflicts: Daylight without correction — the image goes strongly blue (unless you want that)
Clean/precise rendering — halation is inherently soft and glowing
Bright highlights near edges — halation can be extreme and distracting
Natural/documentary — the halation is an obvious stylistic signature
terms.example: CineStill 800T + nighttime city + neon signs + wet streets → halation halos around every light source, warm neon against cool shadows, reflections in puddles glowing red, cinematic dream

terms.name: Lomography Films (Various)
terms.what: A family of experimental and novelty films from the Lomography brand — including high-saturation color stocks, redscale (film loaded backwards for red cast), purple-tinted stocks, and extreme-speed options.
terms.effect: Varies by stock, but the common thread is intentional imperfection and experimentation. Colors are often cross-processed, shifted, or oversaturated. Grain varies. The brand philosophy is "don't think, just shoot" — the aesthetic is deliberately lo-fi, experimental, and accident-embracing.
pairs: Experimental/art photography — the unpredictability is the point
Lo-fi aesthetic — plastic cameras, light leaks, soft focus
Bright/saturated subjects — the film amplifies color weirdness
Cross-processing — many Lomo stocks are designed for it
conflicts: Predictable, controlled results — Lomo is unpredictable by design
Professional/commercial — too inconsistent
Natural color — Lomo stocks shift color deliberately

terms.name: Film Grain
terms.what: Visible particles of metallic silver (B&W) or dye clouds (color) in the developed image. Caused by the random distribution of silver halide crystals in the emulsion. Larger crystals = more light sensitivity = more visible grain.
terms.effect: Adds organic texture and a sense of physical reality. Fine grain (low ISO) is smooth and barely visible. Coarse grain (high ISO, pushed processing) is chunky and dominant. Grain varies frame to frame — unlike digital noise, it's never perfectly uniform. It reads as "analog," "real," and "tactile."
pairs: Any film stock reference — grain is inherent to film
B&W photography — grain and monochrome are deeply linked
Vintage/nostalgic mood — grain signals a physical, pre-digital medium
Underexposure — shadow grain is more visible and textured
Push processing — amplifies grain significantly
conflicts: Ultra-clean digital rendering — grain and digital sharpness fight
Smooth skin/beauty — grain adds texture to everything including skin
Vector/flat illustration styles — grain is photographic, not graphic

terms.name: Light Leaks
terms.what: Unintended light entering the camera body through gaps in the housing, fogging portions of the film with streaks, washes, or patches of color (often amber, red, or magenta).
terms.effect: Warm color washes, typically at the edges or corners of the frame. Streaks of amber or red cutting across the image. Some frames may be heavily fogged, others barely touched. The effect is unpredictable and accidental — every light leak is unique.
pairs: Disposable/toy camera aesthetic — light leaks are a hallmark of cheap cameras
Lomography — the brand embraces light leaks
Warm/nostalgic mood — the color washes add warmth
Double exposure — both are "accidents" of the medium
conflicts: Controlled/precise imagery — light leaks are chaos
Cool color palettes — the leaks are typically warm
Professional/commercial — reads as accidental (unless deliberately stylized)

terms.name: Lens Flare
terms.what: Light scattering inside the lens when a bright source (sun, lamp) hits the glass directly or from just outside the frame. Caused by internal reflections between lens elements. Multi-coated lenses reduce it; vintage/uncoated lenses amplify it.
terms.effect: Streaks, hexagonal or circular ghost shapes, overall haze/wash that reduces contrast, and warm color shifts. The shape of flare elements is determined by the aperture blade count (hexagonal from 6 blades, octagonal from 8). Anamorphic cinema lenses produce distinctive horizontal streak flares.
pairs: Backlit golden hour — shooting toward the sun produces natural flare
Vintage lenses — older coatings produce more flare
Dreamy/romantic mood — the haze and warmth soften the image
Anamorphic/cinematic — horizontal flare streaks signal cinema
Warm tones — flare adds warmth and reduces contrast
conflicts: Sharp/contrasty rendering — flare reduces contrast and adds haze
Cool/clinical tones — flare is warm
Precise control — flare is somewhat unpredictable
terms.example: Lens flare + backlit golden hour + vintage lens + portrait → warm haze washing across the frame, circular ghosts, reduced contrast, dreamy romantic quality

terms.name: Halation
terms.what: A glow or halo around bright highlights on film, caused by light passing through the emulsion, reflecting off the film base, and scattering back into the red-sensitive layer. The anti-halation backing on most film absorbs this; removing it (as CineStill does) creates pronounced halation.
terms.effect: Soft red/orange glow radiating outward from bright light sources — neon signs, candles, street lights, any specular highlight. The glow bleeds into surrounding areas, creating an ethereal, dreamy quality. Different from lens flare (which is in the lens); halation is in the film itself.
pairs: CineStill 800T — the film most associated with halation
Nighttime/artificial light — bright sources against dark areas maximize the effect
Neon signs — the iconic halation subject
Cinematic mood — halation reads as filmic and dreamlike
Warm highlights — the red channel glow amplifies warmth
conflicts: Clean/precise highlights — halation is inherently soft and bloomy
Daytime/even lighting — needs bright point sources against darkness
Sharp detail in highlight areas — halation obscures it

terms.name: Vignetting
terms.what: Darkening at the corners and edges of the frame relative to the center. Caused by light falloff at the lens periphery (natural), lens hood/filter obstruction (mechanical), or internal lens element shading (optical). Can be reduced by stopping down 2-3 stops.
terms.effect: A natural frame-within-a-frame that draws attention to the center. The darkened edges create a tunnel or spotlight effect. Subtle vignetting feels natural and barely noticed. Heavy vignetting feels vintage, lo-fi, or deliberately moody.
pairs: Centered subjects — vignetting reinforces center focus
Vintage/retro aesthetic — vignetting signals old lenses and old processes
Portraits — the darkened edges frame the face
Wide-open aperture — vignetting is strongest wide open, decreasing as you stop down
conflicts: Edge-to-edge sharpness and brightness — vignetting literally darkens the edges
Panoramic/wide compositions where the edges matter
Modern/clean aesthetic — vignetting reads as vintage

terms.name: Chromatic Aberration
terms.what: Color fringing caused by a lens's failure to focus all wavelengths at the same point. Different colors of light refract at slightly different angles, creating colored outlines around high-contrast edges — typically purple/magenta or green.
terms.effect: Colored fringing, most visible at high-contrast boundaries (dark branches against bright sky, text against white). Lateral CA appears at frame edges; longitudinal CA appears as color shifts in out-of-focus areas. Subtle CA reads as vintage/optically imperfect. Heavy CA is distracting.
pairs: Vintage lens aesthetic — old lenses have more CA
Slight optical imperfection — a touch of CA adds analog character
Wide-open aperture — CA is strongest at wide apertures
Lo-fi/disposable camera look — cheap plastic lenses produce heavy CA
conflicts: Clean/precise rendering — CA is a flaw
Modern lens quality — good modern lenses minimize CA
Heavy amounts — a little adds character, a lot is distracting

terms.name: Motion Blur
terms.what: Blurring caused by movement during exposure — either the subject moving or the camera moving (or both). Longer shutter speeds increase blur.
terms.effect: Streaks and smears in the direction of movement. A moving subject becomes a ghost while static elements stay sharp (if camera is still). A moving camera blurs everything while a flash-frozen subject stays sharp (panning). Motion blur conveys speed, energy, and the passage of time.
pairs: Long exposure — intentional creative blur
Panning — subject sharp, background streaked
Action/sports — conveying speed
Nighttime — car light trails, crowd movement
Direct flash + slow shutter — sharp flash-frozen subject with ghosted ambient blur behind it
conflicts: Sharp, frozen detail — motion blur is the opposite
Static/still subjects — no movement to blur
Short shutter speeds — insufficient time for blur to register

terms.name: Double Exposure
terms.what: Two separate images exposed on the same frame of film, overlapping and blending together. Can be done intentionally in-camera or by rewinding and re-exposing the roll.
terms.effect: Ghostly overlap of two scenes. Bright areas of one image dominate; dark areas allow the other image to show through. Creates surreal, dreamlike composites. The two images blend unpredictably — some areas show one scene, some show the other, some blend both.
pairs: Surreal/dreamlike imagery — the overlap is inherently surreal
Portraits + nature — face overlaid with trees, flowers, landscapes (a classic combo)
Experimental/art photography — the unpredictability is the point
Silhouettes — dark subject shape fills with the second exposure
conflicts: Clarity/readability — two overlapping images compete for attention
Clean composition — double exposure is inherently busy
Precise control — the blend is partially unpredictable

terms.name: Cross Processing
terms.what: Deliberately developing film in the wrong chemistry — typically slide film (E-6) in C-41 negative chemistry, or negative film in E-6 reversal chemistry. The chemical mismatch produces shifted, unnatural colors.
terms.effect: E-6 in C-41 (the common version): boosted contrast, shifted hues, increased saturation with unpredictable color casts — greens go yellow, blues go cyan, skin tones shift toward magenta or yellow. The specific shift depends on the film stock. The look is punchy, contrasty, and deliberately wrong. Peaked in 1990s fashion photography (Nick Knight, Anton Corbijn).
pairs: Fashion editorial — the shifted colors are deliberately stylized
1990s aesthetic — cross processing defines 90s fashion photography
Experimental/art — the unpredictability is creative
High saturation scenes — the processing amplifies vivid color
conflicts: Natural/accurate color — cross processing is the opposite
Predictable results — each stock + chemistry combo produces different shifts
Subtle/muted palettes — cross processing is loud

terms.name: Fuji Pro 400H (Discontinued)
terms.what: Professional color negative, ISO 400. Discontinued 2021. Legendary in wedding/portrait work. The most mourned discontinued film stock of the digital era.
terms.effect: Soft, pastel color rendering. Skin tones lean slightly cool/pink rather than warm (opposite of Portra's warmth). Greens shift toward mint/sage. Highlights are creamy and smooth. Low contrast. Almost "watercolor" quality. Fine grain for 400 speed.
pairs: Soft natural light, overcast conditions, pastel environments, bridal/editorial portraiture, garden settings, cool-toned subjects.
conflicts: High contrast, punchy saturated color, harsh flash, gritty urban.

terms.name: Kodak Vision3 250D / 500T (Cinema Stocks)
terms.what: Professional motion picture film. 250D = daylight-balanced, clean natural color. 500T = tungsten-balanced, the most widely used cinema stock in the world. The film behind most modern films shot on celluloid.
terms.effect: 250D — clean, slightly warm, moderate grain, excellent highlight rolloff. The "this looks like a proper movie" baseline. 500T — slightly more grain, beautiful under artificial/mixed light, the specific cinema magic. Warm under tungsten; cool/blue in unfiltered daylight.
pairs: Cinematic compositions, narrative scenes, professional lighting, any genre. "Shot on 500T" is powerful shorthand for cinematic quality.
conflicts: Lo-fi (too polished), vintage/retro (modern stocks), heavily stylized grades (the natural rendering fights extreme manipulation).

terms.name: Kodak T-Max 100/400
terms.what: Modern tabular-grain (T-grain) B&W films. Sharper and finer-grained than traditional Tri-X/HP5. The "clinical" B&W option.
terms.effect: T-Max 100 — extremely fine grain, sharp, slightly cooler/more neutral tone. T-Max 400 — noticeably finer grain than Tri-X at the same speed. More "modern" and less "characterful." Sharper but with less romantic grain texture.
pairs: Fashion B&W, architectural photography, clean modern monochrome, technical work.
conflicts: Vintage/nostalgic (too modern-feeling), gritty photojournalism (too clean), expressionist grain (too refined).

terms.name: Ilford Pan F Plus 50
terms.what: Ultra-fine grain, ultra-slow (ISO 50) B&W film. The sharpest, most detailed traditional B&W available.
terms.effect: Almost grainless at normal print sizes. Extremely fine detail. Smooth, long tonal range. Can feel almost too clean — lacks the "character" grain of faster films. The large-format look on 35mm.
pairs: Studio portraiture, still life, architecture, any subject where detail and smoothness matter.
conflicts: Gritty/street aesthetics, heavy grain, low light (needs lots of light), lo-fi.

terms.name: Agfa Vista / Agfa Color
terms.what: Budget-to-mid-range European consumer color films. Agfa Vista 200/400 were staples with a distinctive color palette.
terms.effect: Slightly muted, earthy. Less saturated than Kodak consumer films. Greens lean olive/muted. Reds go slightly brick. A distinctly "European" color quality. Warmer overall but without Kodak's golden warmth.
pairs: European street photography, documentary, autumn/earth-toned scenes, muted vintage aesthetics.
conflicts: Vivid tropical color, clean modern looks, high-saturation subjects.

terms.name: Fomapan 100/200/400
terms.what: Czech-made B&W film by Foma Bohemia. Budget-priced with distinctive character. Pronounced, chunky grain especially at 400.
terms.effect: Heavy, clumpy grain (especially 400). Lower resolving power than Ilford/Kodak. Compressed tonal range. The grain has a specific "clumpy" quality different from Tri-X or HP5. Feels older, more Eastern European.
pairs: Lo-fi photography, Eastern European aesthetic, street photography, moody/atmospheric work, punk/DIY.
conflicts: Clean precision, fine art smoothness, commercial polish.

terms.name: Expired Film Look
terms.what: The specific color shifts and degradation from film aging past its expiration date. Different stocks degrade differently depending on storage.
terms.effect: Color shifts (often toward magenta, green, or amber). Increased grain. Reduced contrast. Base fog (milky shadows). Unpredictable color casts. Reduced sensitivity. The older and worse the storage, the more extreme the effects.
pairs: Nostalgic/vintage aesthetics, dreamlike imagery, lo-fi, Lomography, psychedelic/surreal subjects.
conflicts: Color accuracy, commercial work, clean modern aesthetics, predictable results.

groups.name: Complementary Grade Combos (Beyond Teal & Orange)
groups.note: Named complementary color grade pairings used in cinema: Each pairing creates a distinct emotional register. Specifying the combination in a prompt is more effective than just "cinematic color grade."

terms.name: Complementary Colors
terms.what: Two colors opposite each other on the color wheel — red/green, blue/orange, yellow/purple. Maximum color contrast.
terms.effect: High visual tension and energy. Each color makes the other appear more vivid. The contrast is eye-catching and dynamic. The most common complementary pairing in cinema is **teal and orange** (skin tones are warm/orange, shadows and backgrounds are pushed toward teal), which became the dominant Hollywood color grade in the 2010s.
pairs: High-energy/dynamic scenes — the contrast demands attention
Fashion editorial — bold color contrast reads as stylish
Teal and orange specifically — cinematic, commercially proven, flattering to skin
Neon lighting — colored lights naturally create complementary zones
Sunset/golden hour against blue sky — nature's complementary palette
conflicts: Harmonious/calm mood — complementary colors create tension, not peace
Monochromatic palettes — the opposite approach
Subtle/understated color — complementary is inherently loud
terms.example: Teal and orange grade + cinematic lighting + portrait + shallow depth of field → warm skin tones against cool teal shadows, Hollywood blockbuster color science

terms.name: Analogous Colors
terms.what: Colors adjacent on the color wheel — blue/blue-green/green, red/orange/yellow. Minimal color contrast.
terms.effect: Harmonious, unified, cohesive. The image feels like it belongs to a single color family. Calm and pleasing without the tension of complementary contrast. The lack of color opposition creates a meditative, immersive quality.
pairs: Calm/serene mood — the harmony soothes
Nature/landscape — forests (green analogous), sunsets (warm analogous), ocean (blue analogous)
Monochromatic-adjacent work — almost single-hue
Muted/pastel palettes — analogous colors in low saturation
conflicts: High energy/contrast — analogous is too calm
Subject separation — similar colors make foreground/background blend
Bold graphic statements — not enough contrast
terms.example: Blue-green analogous palette + overcast seascape + muted tones → ocean, sky, and rocks all in the same cool color family, meditative, unified

terms.name: Split Complementary
terms.what: One base color paired with the two colors flanking its complement — e.g., blue paired with yellow-orange and red-orange instead of just orange.
terms.effect: High contrast like complementary, but more nuanced and less aggressive. The two accent colors create variety while still opposing the base. More sophisticated than straight complementary.
pairs: Fashion/editorial — more interesting color tension than simple complementary
Complex scenes with multiple color elements — the three-color structure organizes them
Stylized/art-directed imagery — the deliberate palette reads as intentional
conflicts: Simplicity — three deliberate colors is more complex than two
Natural/ungraded imagery — split complementary is a conscious choice

terms.name: Triadic
terms.what: Three colors equally spaced around the color wheel — red/yellow/blue (primary triad), orange/green/purple (secondary triad).
terms.effect: Vibrant, balanced, energetic. Each color gets equal weight. The balance prevents any single color from dominating. Reads as playful, graphic, or pop-art-influenced.
pairs: Graphic design / pop art — bold, balanced color
Children's/playful imagery — the vibrancy reads as fun
Fashion with bold color blocking — each piece a different triad member
Saturated palettes — triadic needs saturation to read
conflicts: Muted/desaturated palettes — triadic needs vibrancy
Single-mood imagery — three colors pull in three directions
Realism — nature rarely arranges itself in perfect triads

terms.name: Monochromatic
terms.what: Variations of a single hue — different saturations and values of the same color. A blue image with navy shadows and powder blue highlights is monochromatic.
terms.effect: Unified, immersive, stylized. The single-hue restriction creates a strong mood — blue monochrome feels cold, red feels intense, green feels organic. The viewer is bathed in the color. Form, texture, and light do the compositional work since color contrast is removed.
pairs: Strong mood/atmosphere — the color dominates and sets the emotion
Neon/colored gel lighting — a single color light source creates natural monochrome
Graphic/stylized imagery — the restriction is a design choice
B&W toning (sepia, cyanotype) — monochromatic by nature
conflicts: Color variety/contrast — monochromatic eliminates it
Natural/realistic rendering — the world isn't one color
Subject separation via color — everything is the same hue
terms.example: Blue monochromatic + nighttime + single cool light source + portrait → face in shades of blue, navy shadows, powder highlights, cold and atmospheric

terms.name: Teal and Orange (Hollywood Grade)
terms.what: The dominant color grade of 2010s blockbuster cinema. Push shadows and backgrounds toward teal/cyan, push skin tones and highlights toward warm orange/amber. Complementary color contrast.
terms.effect: Cinematic, commercial, polished. Skin pops against cool backgrounds. Faces look warm and alive. The overall image has a high-production-value sheen. So ubiquitous it's become the default "cinematic" look.
pairs: Any scene with skin tones — the grade is designed around warm skin vs cool surroundings
Action/blockbuster aesthetic — the association is baked in
Three-point or dramatic lighting — the grade amplifies light/shadow color separation
Modern commercial work — the most commercially safe color grade
conflicts: Naturalistic color — teal and orange is an obvious manipulation
Vintage/film stock looks — too modern and digital
Warm-overall or cool-overall palettes — T&O requires both temperatures

terms.name: Desaturated / Muted
terms.what: Overall color saturation reduced. Colors are present but quieted — grays, dusty pastels, faded tones. Not black and white, but moving toward it.
terms.effect: Somber, serious, introspective. The reduced color removes vibrancy and energy, creating a contemplative or melancholy quality. Common in drama, war films, and prestige television. David Fincher's grade (Se7en, Fight Club, Zodiac) is the reference point — green-tinted desaturation that feels oppressive and clinical.
pairs: Drama/thriller — desaturation creates tension and seriousness
Overcast/gray environments — the grade matches the light
Cold/clinical mood — the lack of color warmth feels detached
Gritty/realistic subject matter — war, crime, poverty
Green or blue tint — desaturation plus a single color push
conflicts: Vibrant/energetic mood — too drained
Warm/inviting feeling — desaturation removes warmth
Fashion/beauty — too muted for most commercial use
terms.example: Desaturated + slight green tint + overcast + urban environment → Fincher-esque clinical mood, colors present but suppressed, everything feels slightly wrong

terms.name: Warm Vintage / Faded
terms.what: Lifted shadows (blacks don't go fully black, they fade to dark brown/gray), warm overall tint, reduced contrast, slightly desaturated midtones. The "Instagram filter" look, but also the look of aged or printed photographs.
terms.effect: Nostalgic, soft, romantic. The lifted shadows remove harshness. The warm tint adds comfort. The reduced contrast feels gentle. Reads as memory, nostalgia, or a curated past.
pairs: Lifestyle/wedding photography — the warmth and softness flatter
Golden hour — warm grade + warm light compounds the warmth
Film stock references (Portra, Gold) — the warm vintage grade mimics film characteristics
Soft/diffused light — the grade's gentleness matches soft light
conflicts: Crisp/modern rendering — too soft and warm
High contrast drama — the lifted shadows remove it
Cool/clinical tones — too warm

terms.name: Bleach Bypass / Silver Retention
terms.what: A photochemical technique (or digital emulation) where the silver in the film isn't fully removed during processing, leaving metallic silver over the color dye. Originally a lab technique, now commonly emulated digitally.
terms.effect: Reduced saturation with increased contrast — colors are muted but blacks are deep and highlights are bright. Slightly metallic, desaturated, gritty quality. The image feels simultaneously high-contrast and low-color. Used in Saving Private Ryan, Minority Report, and many war/action films.
pairs: War/combat imagery — the gritty desaturation is genre-defining
Action/thriller — high contrast + low saturation = tension
Hard/directional lighting — the contrast amplifies dramatic light
Gritty realism — the metallic quality feels raw
conflicts: Vivid color — bleach bypass suppresses it
Soft/romantic mood — too harsh and contrasty
Beauty/fashion — too desaturated and gritty
terms.example: Bleach bypass + hard side light + war scene + desaturated → deep blacks, muted colors, metallic sheen on skin, high contrast, Saving Private Ryan intensity

terms.name: Day for Night
terms.what: A technique of shooting in daylight and grading the footage to appear as nighttime — heavy blue tint, crushed blacks, reduced exposure.
terms.effect: An artificial nighttime look with an obviously stylized quality. The blue tint is deeper than real night. Shadows are exaggerated. Some detail remains visible that would be lost in actual darkness. Reads as theatrical or fantastical rather than realistically nocturnal.
pairs: Fantasy/stylized scenes — the obvious artifice works for non-realistic content
Deep blue color grading — the defining color
Moonlit exterior scenes — the intended simulation
conflicts: Realistic nighttime — real night is darker and less uniformly blue
Warm tones — day for night is exclusively cool/blue
Interior scenes — the technique is designed for exteriors

terms.name: Cross-Processed Look
terms.what: Digital emulation of chemical cross-processing (see Film Stocks & Analog). Shifted hues, boosted saturation, unnatural color casts — typically greens shift yellow, shadows go teal, highlights go warm.
terms.effect: Punchy, contrasty, color-shifted. The colors feel "wrong" in an energetic way. Greens go sickly, skin tones shift toward yellow or magenta. The 1990s fashion photography look.
pairs: Fashion editorial — the shifted colors are deliberately stylized
1990s aesthetic — the era's defining look
High saturation scenes — amplifies the weirdness
Punchy/editorial energy — reads as confident and stylish
conflicts: Natural color accuracy — the opposite
Subtle/quiet mood — cross-process is loud
Warm/cozy tones — the color shifts are unpredictable

terms.name: Black and White
terms.what: Complete removal of color information. The image exists only as values of light and dark. The oldest and most fundamental photographic treatment.
terms.effect: Abstracts from reality. Removes the distraction of color, emphasizing form, texture, contrast, light, and composition. Emotions feel heightened because the viewer processes the image differently — it's already one step removed from reality. Reads as serious, artistic, timeless, or dramatic.
pairs: Hard directional light — B&W amplifies the contrast and shadow drama
Strong textures — grain, skin texture, fabric, stone all read powerfully in monochrome
High contrast — deep blacks + bright whites = graphic impact
Portraiture — the emphasis on form and light over color is flattering and expressive
Film grain — B&W grain has an iconic quality
conflicts: Color-dependent subjects — fashion where the clothing color matters, food photography
Warm/cool mood distinctions — B&W removes temperature
Subtle color grading — there's no color to grade
terms.example: Black and white + high contrast + hard side light + portrait + visible grain → dramatic, timeless, textural, form and light doing all the work

terms.name: Sepia Tone
terms.what: B&W image toned warm brown, named after cuttlefish ink pigment. Originally a chemical darkroom process that also improved print longevity. Now universally associated with antique photographs.
terms.effect: Warm, aged, antique. The brown tone adds warmth to monochrome without introducing full color. Reads as historical, nostalgic, or deliberately vintage. The association with old photographs is so strong that sepia immediately signals "the past."
pairs: Period/historical subjects — the aging effect matches
Soft/warm lighting — reinforces the warmth
Portraiture — warm-toned monochrome is flattering
Vintage texture (grain, scratches, vignetting) — the full aged-photo package
conflicts: Modern/contemporary subjects — sepia looks backward, not forward
Cool mood — sepia is inherently warm
Vivid/energetic feeling — sepia is quiet and reflective

terms.name: Cyanotype (Blue Tone)
terms.what: Monochrome image toned in Prussian blue. Originally an iron-salt photographic printing process invented in 1842 (the "blueprint" is a cyanotype). The distinctive deep blue with white highlights.
terms.effect: Cool, ethereal, otherworldly. The blue tone creates a dreamlike or melancholic quality. Reads as historical (but different from sepia — industrial/scientific rather than portrait/domestic), artistic, or deliberately stylized. The blue-and-white palette is striking and graphic.
pairs: Botanical/nature subjects — the original cyanotypes were botanical prints
Cool/melancholic mood — the blue is inherently cold
Graphic compositions — the high-contrast blue and white is bold
Historical/artistic reference — signals knowledge of photographic history
conflicts: Warm mood — cyanotype is cold
Realistic rendering — the blue is obviously stylized
Subtle/understated treatment — the blue is strong

terms.name: Selenium Tone
terms.what: B&W print toned with selenium, producing a blue-black or slightly purple-cool shift in the shadows. More subtle than sepia or cyanotype. Also increases print archival stability.
terms.effect: Cool-neutral, rich, deep. The shadows gain a subtle blue-black quality that adds depth without an obvious color cast. The most "serious" and subtle of the toning methods. Used in fine art printing for its archival benefits and its slight cool richness.
pairs: Fine art B&W — the subtle tone adds depth without distraction
Rich shadow detail — the selenium shift lives in the darks
High-quality printing — the archival association signals craft
Cool/neutral mood — subtly cool without being as obvious as cyanotype
conflicts: Warm tones — selenium is cool
Obvious stylization — the effect is subtle, not dramatic
Casual/snapshot aesthetic — too refined

terms.name: Duotone
terms.what: Two-color image — a monochrome base with a second color layered over specific tonal ranges. Black + a color (blue, red, gold, etc.) is most common. Originally a printing technique, now a design/photography treatment.
terms.effect: Graphic, bold, stylized. The two-color restriction creates a strong visual identity. Different color pairings produce different moods — black + gold feels luxurious, black + red feels intense, black + teal feels modern. The technique bridges B&W and full color — more expressive than monochrome, more controlled than full color.
pairs: Graphic design / poster aesthetic — duotone is a design tool
Bold/high-contrast compositions — the restriction demands strong form
Brand identity — the two-color scheme can match brand colors
Editorial/magazine layout — graphic and eye-catching
Portraits — the two-color treatment is striking on faces
conflicts: Natural/realistic color — duotone is obviously artificial
Subtle tonal work — duotone is bold, not subtle
Complex multi-color scenes — the restriction eliminates variety
terms.example: Duotone (black + electric blue) + high contrast portrait + hard light → graphic, modern, bold, face rendered in deep black shadows and vivid blue highlights

terms.name: High Saturation
terms.what: Colors pushed to maximum vibrancy. Every hue is as intense as possible.
terms.effect: Vivid, energetic, overwhelming. The image buzzes with color energy. Can feel tropical, psychedelic, pop-art, or commercial depending on the palette. Common in advertising, music videos, and social media content.
pairs: Bright/direct lighting — saturation needs light to pop
Bold/graphic compositions — the intensity matches visual boldness
Fashion with colorful clothing — each piece screams its color
Tropical/summer scenes — bright sun + saturated = vacation energy
Pop art / Warhol-esque treatment — hyper-saturation is pop art
conflicts: Subtle/quiet mood — too loud
Natural/realistic rendering — over-saturation is obviously processed
Skin tone accuracy — pushing saturation makes skin look unnatural

terms.name: Pastel / Low Saturation + High Value
terms.what: Colors present but softened — low saturation combined with lifted exposure. Pinks, powder blues, soft yellows, lavender. The candy-colored, soft aesthetic.
terms.effect: Gentle, dreamy, feminine (in traditional coding), delicate. The soft colors feel like they're seen through gauze. Reads as romantic, youthful, or fashion-editorial in certain contexts. The absence of deep blacks or vivid color creates an airy, floating quality.
pairs: Soft/diffused light — the light quality matches the color softness
Fashion/beauty — the pastel palette is commercially ubiquitous
Overexposed highlights — the blown whites add to the airiness
Minimal compositions — pastel + negative space = calm
Spring/floral subjects — pastels are the colors of spring
conflicts: Drama/intensity — too soft
High contrast — pastels need low contrast to exist
Gritty/raw aesthetic — the opposite energy
terms.example: Pastel palette + soft diffused light + fashion subject + minimal background + slight overexposure → airy, dreamy, soft pink and lavender tones, blown white highlights, editorial calm

terms.name: Split Toning
terms.what: Assigning different color hues to highlights and shadows independently. Classic: warm amber highlights + cool blue shadows. A precise tool for mood control.
terms.effect: Sophisticated, stylized mood without flattening contrast. The color split creates visual temperature tension — warm where light falls, cool where shadow lives. Reads as editorial, polished, cinematic.
pairs: Portrait photography — the warm/cool split flatters skin
Golden hour — amber highlights amplify the warmth naturally
Film emulation — many film stocks have inherent split toning
Desaturated base images — split toning works on muted images
conflicts: Heavy overall saturation — fights the subtlety
Neon/rainbow palettes — too many colors competing
Monochrome — split toning needs a color-capable image

terms.name: Color Blocking
terms.what: Large, flat areas of bold, contrasting solid color. Mondrian in photography. The design principle applied to the whole frame.
terms.effect: Graphic, bold, modern, fashion-forward. Strong visual impact. Flattens depth — the bold planes read as design rather than space. Reads as editorial, pop, confident.
pairs: Minimalist composition — clean shapes of color
Fashion photography — bold clothing against bold backgrounds
Flat lighting — even illumination lets the color speak
Pop art — shared bold flat color language
Complementary or triadic color schemes — maximum contrast
conflicts: Photorealism — too graphic and designed
Moody chiaroscuro — needs even light
Natural environments — nature doesn't color-block
Muted/desaturated palettes — needs vivid color

terms.name: Technicolor (Three-Strip)
terms.what: The specific hyper-saturated color process of Golden Age Hollywood (1930s-1960s). Three strips of film captured red, green, blue separately, producing impossibly rich, slightly artificial color. Wizard of Oz, Singin' in the Rain, Gone with the Wind.
terms.effect: Extremely saturated reds and greens. Rich skin tones (slightly ruddy). Deep blacks. A "painted" quality to color — vivid but not harsh. Everything looks slightly more real than real. The warmth and richness are distinctive and instantly recognizable as "old Hollywood color."
pairs: Period costume — the era of Technicolor was the era of glamour
Theatrical lighting — bold production design
Bold production design — saturated sets and costumes
Glamour portraiture — the Hollywood look
conflicts: Natural/documentary — Technicolor is deliberately artificial
Desaturated/muted — the opposite approach
Modern muted grading — Technicolor is vivid
Gritty realism — too beautiful

terms.name: HDR / Tone-Mapped Look
terms.what: The over-processed look from aggressive tone mapping of HDR bracketed exposures. Equalizes all luminance — shadows and highlights both fully visible. The "real estate listing photo" aesthetic.
terms.effect: Halos around edges, hyper-detailed textures, flat-feeling despite visible contrast. Slightly surreal — the eye sees detail everywhere simultaneously, which feels unnatural. The specific "Flickr HDR circa 2010" quality.
pairs: Architecture/real estate — the native format
Landscapes (intentional) — dramatic sky + detailed foreground
Surrealist imagery — the unnatural detail is dreamlike
Tilt-shift — miniature effect + HDR detail is a combination
conflicts: Naturalism — HDR tone mapping is obviously processed
Portraiture — makes skin look terrible
Cinematic looks — too flat and detailed
Elegant/refined aesthetics — too crunchy

terms.name: Matte Painting Color
terms.what: The color quality of traditional hand-painted matte paintings used in classic film VFX. Slightly simplified value range, paint-like blending, subtly artificial but beautiful. Original Star Wars backgrounds, classic Disney mattes.
terms.effect: Slightly hazy atmospheric perspective. Simplified palette compared to reality. Soft edges in distant elements. "Painted reality" quality — real enough to believe but with the warmth and simplification of painted work.
pairs: Fantasy landscapes — the epic vista
Golden hour lighting — warm, atmospheric
Classic cinema aesthetic — the era of physical matte paintings
Illustrated realism — the bridge between photo and painting
conflicts: Photorealism — the painterly simplification gives it away
Harsh direct lighting — mattes are atmospheric
Modern CGI look — different visual quality entirely
Documentary — too polished and idealized

terms.name: Negative Scan Look
terms.what: The specific aesthetic of scanning color negative film, including process artifacts. Orange mask warm cast, lifted blacks, and the character of different scanners.
terms.effect: **Frontier scan** — punchier contrast, more saturated, slightly cooler. "Instagram before Instagram." **Noritsu scan** — warmer, softer, more muted contrast. Skin tones warmer and more flattering. Both share: slightly lifted blacks (shadows don't reach true black), organic warmth, slight imperfection.
pairs: Lifestyle/portrait photography — the warm organic quality
Wedding photography — the romantic warmth
Street photography — authentic analog feel
Warm natural light — the scan character amplifies warmth
conflicts: Clinical precision — the scan adds character/imperfection
Digital sharpness — analog scans have inherent softness
Futuristic aesthetics — too analog and warm
High contrast B&W — different process entirely

terms.name: Amber + Steel Blue
terms.effect: warmer, less aggressive. Period dramas. The English Patient.

terms.name: Magenta + Green
terms.effect: unsettling, surreal. Horror, sci-fi. Spring Breakers, Refn films.

terms.name: Gold + Deep Blue
terms.effect: regal, epic. Fantasy, historical. Gladiator, Lord of the Rings.

terms.name: Teal + Pink/Magenta
terms.effect: vaporwave-adjacent. Drive, Miami Vice.

terms.name: Yellow-Green + Purple
terms.effect: toxic, alien. Alien franchise, Annihilation.

terms.name: Copper + Slate
terms.effect: industrial, restrained. Sicario, Prisoners.

terms.name: Cream + Navy
terms.effect: classic, clean, editorial. Fashion, lifestyle.

groups.name: Leather (Specific Types)
groups.note: Each type reads completely differently. Always specify which — "leather texture" alone defaults to generic smooth brown.

groups.name: Paper Textures
groups.note: Each paper type completely changes the mood of anything printed on or placed against it.

groups.name: Foil / Leaf
groups.note: Gold leaf has organic irregularity; foil is uniform. Both are reflective and luxurious.

terms.name: Matte
terms.what: A surface that scatters reflected light in all directions equally (diffuse reflection). No sheen, no glare, no reflections. Examples: raw concrete, chalk, unfinished wood, matte paper, matte skin (no oil/sweat).
terms.effect: Soft, quiet, unassuming. The surface absorbs attention rather than deflecting it. Colors appear more even across the surface since there are no bright specular highlights. Textures are visible but gentle. Reads as understated, organic, or deliberately controlled.
pairs: Soft/diffused lighting — matte surfaces don't fight soft light
Minimal/modern aesthetics — matte is the surface of quiet design
Product photography with muted palettes — matte objects in matte light
Scandinavian design — matte wood, linen, ceramic
Flat lay compositions — matte surfaces don't create distracting reflections
conflicts: Glamour/luxury — matte is too quiet (unless deliberately understated luxury)
Dramatic specular highlights — matte surfaces don't produce them
Wet/reflective aesthetics — the opposite surface quality
terms.example: Matte ceramic + matte linen + soft diffused light + desaturated palette → quiet, tactile, understated, every surface absorbs light evenly

terms.name: Glossy / Polished
terms.what: A smooth surface that produces specular reflections — clear, mirror-like bouncing of light. Examples: polished metal, wet surfaces, lacquered wood, glossy paper, glass, patent leather.
terms.effect: Bright specular highlights, clear reflections of surrounding environment, strong contrast between highlight and shadow on the surface. Reads as high-end, polished, luxurious, or wet. The highlights catch the eye and create visual energy.
pairs: Hard/directional lighting — creates defined specular highlights
Product photography — the polish signals quality and finish
Luxury/fashion — glossy surfaces read as expensive
Dark backgrounds — specular highlights pop against darkness
Controlled studio light — precise highlights on precise surfaces
conflicts: Matte/organic aesthetics — too reflective
Soft/diffused light — doesn't produce the strong highlights glossy needs
Rustic/natural mood — too polished
terms.example: Glossy black lacquer surface + hard key light + product on top + dark background → sharp specular highlight streaking across the surface, product reflected, luxury and precision

terms.name: Satin / Semi-Gloss
terms.what: Between matte and glossy — a soft sheen that produces diffused highlights rather than sharp reflections. Examples: silk fabric, brushed metal, satin-finish paint, healthy skin.
terms.effect: Soft glow rather than sharp reflection. Highlights are broader and gentler than on glossy surfaces. The surface catches light without creating distracting mirror reflections. Reads as refined, healthy, premium.
pairs: Beauty/skin photography — healthy skin has a satin quality
Soft directional light — produces broad, flattering highlights
Fabric/textile focus — silk, satin, charmeuse have this quality
Warm tones — satin highlights pick up light color beautifully
conflicts: Maximum reflectivity — satin is softer than full gloss
Completely matte — satin has some sheen
Gritty/rough textures — satin is smooth

terms.name: Metallic
terms.what: The specific reflective quality of metals — high specular reflection combined with the material's own color tinting the reflection. Gold reflects warm, chrome reflects neutral, copper reflects warm-pink, brushed aluminum scatters.
